still confirm with your own split test.","Note the source's general claim that anything under 10% off is less effective, and treat it as a starting hypothesis for testing rather than a rule.","When the offer changes, update the headline, CTA button and any teaser/quiz copy so the promise is consistent across every step of the form."],"caveats":["The sub-10% and $200 AOV figures are the source's heuristics, not established benchmarks — discount depth must be validated against your own margin structure.","Aggressive discounting can train customers to wait for discounts and compress margin; EU privacy rules are explicitly said to be different — confirm with counsel for your markets.","The two-option microcopy relies on cited research the source does not name; test it on your own audience."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","signup-form","conversion-optimization","copywriting","offer-design","list-growth"]},{"title":"Micro-Commitment (Micro-Yes) Step Before the Email Field","summary":"Insert a one-question yes/no step before the email field to create commitment, then measure whether it lifts total signups for your audience.","use_when":"Optimizing the opt-in form flow on a popup to raise email capture rate.","steps":["Clone the email opt-in step and place a stripped-down version before it: remove the input field, change the primary CTA to something like 'Yes please', and keep a secondary 'No thanks'.","Frame the question as the offer, e.g. 'Do you want 20% off your first order?', with emphasis on the number.","Clicking 'Yes please' advances to the email field step; Too short disrupts the visit and reads as spam; too long means fewer visitors ever see the form, so a high signup rate on tiny volume still yields few subscribers.","Layer a scroll condition, with about 60% as the source's starting point, and optionally a minimum pages-viewed condition. The source leaves these conditions non-mandatory (AND logic off).","Handle repeat exposure: set the closed form to re-display after about 3 days instead of the default 5.","Build one desktop-only form and one mobile-only form rather than a single responsive form, so layout, timing and copy can differ by device and A/B results are not mixed.","On mobile, disable the exit-intent trigger — the source calls mobile exit intent unreliable and says it fires when people are not leaving, harming experience.","Exclude existing subscribers (e.g. 'don't show to existing profiles'), the cart page and the checkout page so visitors already about to purchase are not offered a discount, and exclude wholesale or other non-retail pages.","If you only ship to one country, restrict display by location so the offer is relevant."],"caveats":["The 6-second delay, 4–12 second range, 60% scroll and 3-day re-show are the source's recommended starting points, framed as things to split test rather than fixed rules.","Excluding the cart and checkout pages is a deliberate choice to protect full-price orders; style it for contrast (e.g. black background, white centered text).","On mobile, switch the teaser to a circle and shorten the text so it does not occupy the full bottom bar — the source notes that stacked elements such as loyalty promotions can collide with a full-width bar.","Verify the teaser does not overlap checkout, cart or other persistent UI.","Split test teaser present versus absent; the source reports the teaser lifts both signup rate and the absolute number of subscribers."],"caveats":["The claim that the teaser lifts both rate and absolute subscribers comes from the source's own testing and is not quantified.","If your storefront already has several floating elements, a persistent teaser may add clutter; the source itself acknowledges this case."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","signup-form","list-growth","conversion-optimization","mobile","merchandising"]},{"title":"Post-Opt-In Success Page: Withhold the Code, Train Email Opens","summary":"Route new subscribers to their inbox for the discount instead of displaying it on the success page, to protect first-email engagement signals.","use_when":"Writing the success/confirmation screen copy that appears after a visitor submits their email on the opt-in form.","steps":["Make the success page visually identical to the form: same logo, same fonts, same colours.","Write a future-pacing headline such as 'Your discount code is on its way' rather than revealing the code.","Add instructions: check your inbox for the confirmation message containing the discount code.","Add the fallback line: if no email arrives within 5 minutes, check your spam folder — the source says this pre-empts support tickets caused by deliverability issues.","The source deliberately does not display the discount code on this page, arguing it removes any reason to open the first welcome email; a low open rate on a brand-new subscriber's very first email is a negative signal to inbox providers.","Test the alternative if you have strong reason to believe instant code delivery converts better for your audience; the source acknowledges this is an active industry debate and states its own position rather than a universal rule."],"caveats":["Holding back the code risks losing subscribers who never check email; this is the deliberate trade-off the source chooses, not a proven best practice.","The deliverability reasoning is the presenter's explanation, not a documented provider policy."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","signup-form","deliverability","welcome-flow","retention","list-growth"]},{"title":"Separate Desktop and Mobile Signup Forms","summary":"Clone the desktop form into a dedicated mobile form and fix the specific elements that break at small sizes.","use_when":"Adapting an existing opt-in popup for mobile traffic, or before starting device-level A/B tests.","steps":["Clone the desktop form, name it as the mobile version, and set device targeting to mobile only; leave the original on desktop only.","Remove the exit-intent rule on mobile because the trigger is unreliable there.","Audit every element for size: check that fonts are legible and that nothing overflows the viewport.","Increase the call-to-action button height (the source uses about 70 px) and raise CTA label size (about 30 px) so the button is comfortably tappable.","Raise secondary action text (e.g. 'No thanks') to about 18 px.","Increase emphasis sizes where the offer number appears inside the form (source uses 60 px in the micro-commitment step).","Raise the input field height (about 70 px) and input text size (about 20 px) via the general styling settings.","Increase success-page body text to about 22 px.","Skip images on mobile entirely where possible, or compress the logo, because mobile load time depends on the visitor's connection — the source says images are a common conversion killer."],"caveats":["Pixel sizes are the source's working values on a specific ESP builder and reproduce that presenter's config, not a universal standard; verify against your own template and your current interface.","Because results can differ by device, keep desktop and mobile tested and reported separately rather than averaging them."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","signup-form","mobile","conversion-optimization","experiment-design","page-speed"]},{"title":"Redirect Your Signup Offer Away From Cart and Checkout Traffic","summary":"Suppress discount popups for visitors in the cart and checkout so you do not discount orders that would have completed at full price."],"use_when":"Configuring URL inclusion and exclusion rules for the opt-in popup on an ecommerce store.","steps":["Exclude the cart page from popup display so a visitor mid-cart is not interrupted or re-priced.","Exclude the checkout page so a visitor about to purchase at full price is not offered a discount.","Exclude wholesale, B2B or other non-retail pages where the consumer offer is irrelevant.","Keep display on product, collection, homepage and content pages where the visitor is still exploring and the capture is additive.","Review exclusions whenever the theme changes URLs or SPAs change the path structure, since URL rules can silently stop matching."],"caveats":["This reduces capture volume in exchange for protecting full-price conversion; if your cart or checkout abandonment is high, test whether the loss of capture outweighs the protection.","Excluding checkout does not solve abandonment — it must be paired with an abandoned-checkout flow."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","signup-form","cart-abandonment","conversion-optimization","popup-targeting","checkout"]},{"title":"Compress Signup Form Images to Protect Load Time","summary":"Run every image used in an opt-in form through compression before uploading, because load time is a major conversion killer.","use_when":"Preparing product or lifestyle imagery for a signup popup, full-page form or landing page opt-in.","steps":["Compress images externally before uploading to the email platform; the source names TinyPNG and Squoosh.","Upload the compressed file to the form builder only after compression, because large originals slow the form down and long load times suppress conversion.","Write descriptive alt text for every image, including the logo — alt text is what visitors see when an image fails to load.","For mobile forms, avoid images altogether and compress the logo if you keep it, since mobile load speed depends on the visitor's connection.","Check that the logo or hero image does not push the email field below the fold on small screens."],"caveats":["Compression tools are third-party products whose interfaces and settings change — verify the current workflow before relying on instructions.","The source claims load time is a major conversion killer but gives no measured threshold for image weight."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","signup-form","page-speed","conversion-optimization","mobile","creative-assets"]},{"title":"Ten Common Signup Form Mistakes to Audit Against","summary":"Audit a live opt-in form against the source's recurring failure modes, led by a weak offer.","use_when":"Reviewing an underperforming opt-in form or onboarding a store's existing email capture setup.","steps":["Offer too weak: if the incentive is not compelling, fix that first — the source ranks it above every design issue.","Asking too much in one step: collect email, phone, first name, birthday and similar data in separate steps; if you collect phone number or other fields, add them after the email step. The source warns that visitors willing to give an email but not a phone number may abandon the whole form, losing the email entirely.","Time delay too short or too long: balance visibility against positive experience (see delay guidance in the timing card).","Form too small: the source's guidance is that a bigger form captures attention better, and suggests testing popup versus full-screen.","Too much copy: no supporting text blocks explaining that subscribers will receive offers and promotions.","Offer missing from the headline: the offer should be the first thing read, not buried in body copy.","'Sign up' / 'subscribe' language in headline or CTA: replace with the benefit.","Single form for both devices: build and test desktop and mobile separately.","Slow-loading form: compress images; skip images on mobile.","Incentive revealed on the success page: direct people to the inbox instead (source's position; an industry debate)."],"caveats":["These are the source's observed common mistakes, not a validated ranking of conversion impact beyond the stated ordering of offer first.","The phone-number advice assumes email is the primary identifier for your program; a strong offer with weak design beats a weak offer with strong design per the source.","Test 2 — micro-commitment step on versus off: usually lifts conversion but not for every audience.","Test 3 — time delay: a shorter delay raises signup rate but lowers total signups, so judge on total signups.","Test 4 — popup versus full-page form: full-page has greater visibility and wins for some brands.","Test 5 — headline copy, e.g. 'Save 20% now', 'Get 20% now', 'Take 20% now', 'Unlock 20% off now', 'Your discount awaits', 'Do you want 20% off?'.","Test 6 — CTA button copy, e.g. 'Save 20% off now', 'Get 20% off now', 'Unlock my discount now', 'Reveal my discount now', 'I want my discount'.","Test 7 — microcopy under the CTA: test variants such as 'No thanks', 'No thanks, I'll pay full price', 'No spam guaranteed', or social proof like 'Rated 4.9/5 by 5,000 customers', and test having microcopy versus none.","Test 8 — colour and design: plain versus fully designed form, light versus dark form, input field colour, CTA colour. Lower leverage than the above.","Test 9 — image versus no image: an image can distract from the form, so test both; also test different images (the source gives a client example where an image with a dog far outperformed one without, and explicitly warns against generalising that).","Test 10 — SMS opt-in angle: same 20%-off question framed for phone capture, a higher discount for SMS than for email (e.g. 10% email vs 20% SMS), or positioning the SMS list as a VIP club."],"caveats":["Priority order is the presenter's ranking of leverage, not a measured effect-size table.","Most variables are low-leverage; do not spend signup-form test volume on colour before offer and flow structure are settled.","Each audience differs, so a variable that wins elsewhere may lose here."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","signup-form","experiment-design","conversion-optimization","offer-design","sms"]},{"title":"Configure a Signup A/B Test: Manual 50/50 and Winner Selection","summary":"Set the traffic split manually rather than automatic so the platform does not call a winner on insufficient volume.","use_when":"Launching an A/B test on a popup or form inside your email platform.","steps":["Create the test from the existing form, name it for the variable under test (e.g. 'offer test').","Set variant A as the current control and variant B as the challenger, then update every dependent element of variant B — for an offer test that means the headline, the email opt-in, the teaser and the form's design copy all reflect the new offer.","In test settings, set the traffic weight to manual 50/50 rather than automatic; it trades speed for the operator's control.","No minimum sample size is given; you must set your own stopping rule before reading results."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","experiment-design","signup-form","measurement","conversion-optimization","platform-tools"]},{"title":"Full-Screen Opt-In Forms and Zero-Party Data Quizzes","summary":"Use full-screen branded popups with a single question to capture intent data alongside the email address.","use_when":"Choosing a capture format, or adding a segmentation question at the point of opt-in for a Shopify store.","steps":["Consider full-screen forms on both desktop and mobile rather than small popups, which the source argues hurt conversion; for a gift-focused store, the recipient.","Use a 'No thanks' exit so the full-screen takeover is escapable.","Pass the zero-party answers through the platform integration into your email list so they become segmentation properties on the subscriber profile.","Review survey-answer performance reporting to see which answers correlate with higher purchase behaviour, then weight acquisition and campaign targeting toward those segments."],"caveats":["Full-screen popups are more intrusive; the source argues the format win justifies it, but this is not presented as a cross-store benchmark.","Collecting a question before the email adds a step; the source argues the micro-commitment outweighs the friction, but it must be tested.","Integration availability and the exact question/report UI vary by platform and change over time — verify the current interface."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","zero-party-data","signup-form","segmentation","list-growth","shopify","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Gamified Opt-In First Steps: Spin-to-Win and Scratch-Off","summary":"Test interactive first steps before the email field, using a guaranteed-win mechanic, and expect different winners per audience.","use_when":"Choosing the opening interaction on a full-screen capture form to raise engagement and signup rate.","steps":["Spin-to-win: configure the wheel so every visitor receives a reward — the wheel always lands on the designated reward slice, and you may display other slices as decoy rewards. the source reports the mini quiz or scratch-off usually win, but says every audience differs.","Judge on total subscribers and downstream revenue, not just the completion rate of the mechanic.","If you already run a strong baseline, test one mechanic at a time so you can attribute the change."],"caveats":["The source relates one brand moving from about 11% to about 14% conversion after adding a scratch-off, and separately a scratch-off revealing a discount; this is a single client anecdote, not a promised result.","The scratch-off is described as a newer feature; availability and behaviour should be verified in the current platform interface.","Decoy reward slices on a rigged wheel create a misleading expectation — weigh the engagement gain against trust and any local consumer-protection rules."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","gamification","signup-form","conversion-optimization","experiment-design","list-growth"]},{"title":"Deliverability Hygiene: Authentication, Engagement Tiers and List Cleaning","summary":"Implement SPF, DKIM and DMARC, segment by engagement recency, and suppress long-inactive subscribers to protect inbox placement.","use_when":"Setting up or auditing sending infrastructure and list health, especially before scaling campaign volume.","steps":["Implement the technical authentication trio — SPF, DKIM and DMARC — on your sending domain so mailbox providers can verify you.","Segment by engagement recency using activity windows; do not judge them purely on attributed revenue in the first days."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","automation","welcome-flow","abandoned-cart","post-purchase","retention","prioritization"]},{"title":"Email Campaign Cadence and Audience Strategy","summary":"Plan campaign volume around a 3–4 per week cadence, sent with a real strategy rather than ad hoc.","use_when":"Setting or reviewing the weekly campaign calendar and checking whether sends are strategic or random.","steps":["Use 3 to 4 campaigns per week as the source's recommended cadence reference point for the campaign layer of the email system.","Ensure campaigns sit on top of a working list-growth and flow layer; the source's stated reason is that most brands are missing key flows, sending without strategy, or treating symptoms, so advanced features amplify a broken base rather than fixing it.","Once the base works, add active gamification (spin-to-win, scratch-offs) and zero-party data collection quizzes to lift engagement and enrich profiles.","Split test distinct desktop and mobile experiences rather than assuming one experience transfers, because results diverge by device.","Route collected zero-party data into segmentation so it drives targeting and campaign decisions instead of sitting unused in the capture tool.","Re-evaluate the tool stack only when a measured gap remains after the fundamentals are in place."],"caveats":["The source is explicit that AI is a speed-and-efficiency layer applied last, not a solution to a missing flow or a deliverability problem.","Tool availability and integration behaviour change frequently; verify current capabilities in the interfaces you use."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","ai","personalization","zero-party-data","strategy","prioritization","experiment-design"]}]}

Implementing technical authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), regularly cleaning unengaged subscribers (suppressing profiles inactive past 180 days), and utilizing engagement-tiered segmentation (14-day, 30-day, 60-day, and 90-day active windows) to maximize primary inbox placement.

Look for. The recommended campaign sending frequency: 3 to 4 campaigns per week. The critical purchase window for welcome flows: the first 72 hours (with day zero driving the highest conversion volume). The core Klaviyo automated flows: Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Abandoned Cart, Abandoned Checkout, and Post-Purchase. The list cleaning benchmark: suppressing unengaged subscribers who have been inactive for 180 days.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 25 to 30.

If you want cla email marketing to drive serious revenue for your store in 2026, you do not need more random tactics. You need the right email system. Because most ecom brands are either missing key flows, sending campaigns without a real strategy, or trying to fix performance issues without understanding what's actually broken underneath. So, in this full email marketing course, I'm going to walk you through the exact setup I'd focus on to build a high performing email system from the ground up. We will start with list growth because none of the rest of this matters if you're not consistently adding new email subscribers to your list. Then we're going to build out the core email flows, layer on campaigns, cover AB testing, segmentation, deliverability, and finally we will discuss how to use AI to make the whole email system faster and smarter. And that order matters because each part affects the next. And by the end of this course, you should be able to look at your own Clavio account and know exactly what to build, what to fix, where the biggest revenue opportunities are. So, let's start at the very beginning, your signup form. So, first of all, why having a high converting pop-up form is so important. Most people who click on your ads and land on your website aren't going to buy straight away. 98% of the people will leave your store without leaving a trace. So, they're just simply browsing, comparing, and just checking your brand out. So without a solid way to capture those people, they're just going to leave your store without leaving a trace and you might never see them again. And of course, you can run some retargeting ads via Facebook or Google, but that's just super expensive to run for your e-commerce store. So this is where a high converting sign form comes into play. So it serves as the gateway to turning those casual visitors into potential customers for your brand. So by capturing their details through an engaging and well-placed signup form, you're not just collecting data, you're creating an opportunity for ongoing communication. This means that you can nurture those leads with your welcome series flow and with your email campaigns. And this way you can build trust with them and guide them towards that first purchase. And from there you can nurture them into a repeat customer. So it's a key tool for lowering your customer acquisition and making sure that the traffic that you're paying for doesn't just vanish. So this is the typical e-commerce funnel that I often see and that's that brands are running top of funnel paid ads. People will visit your website. 2% of them on average will be converting and actually buying from you. But 98% of the people are leaving your store without actually purchasing.
